title: Lotka-Volterra Dynamics and Population Waves
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter finishes the analysis of the two-species Lotka-Volterra competition model started in the previous lecture, then asks two questions that go beyond it: what happens with many competing species, and what happens when competition is non-transitive — a rock-paper-scissors relation among three strategies or species, where no single one dominates. It closes with a different mechanism for spatial spread, the reaction-diffusion population wave. It assumes the two-species Lotka-Volterra competition model itself — the parameters $r_i$, $K_i$, and the competition coefficients $\beta_{ij}$ — together with phase-plane fixed-point analysis (nullclines, eigenvectors, stability), from the class this one continues. ## Recap: the two-species competition model Two species compete when each one's presence lowers the other's per-capita growth rate. Written as a Lotka-Volterra system, $$\dot N_1 = r_1 N_1\left(1-\frac{N_1+\beta_{12}N_2}{K_1}\right), \qquad \dot N_2 = r_2 N_2\left(1-\frac{N_2+\beta_{21}N_1}{K_2}\right),$$ this is competition exactly when $\beta_{12},\beta_{21}>0$: each species' own carrying capacity is diminished by the other species' population, weighted by how strongly it interferes. $\beta_{12}$ says how much species 2 reduces species 1's growth; $\beta_{21}$ says how much species 1 reduces species 2's. There are four possible long-run outcomes, and — as the lecture had already shown for frequency-dependent selection between two strategies within a single species — they turn out to be formally the same four outcomes that show up there. That coincidence is not an accident: there is a general mapping between the Lotka-Volterra competition picture (different species) and the frequency-dependent selection picture (changing strategy frequencies in one, asexually reproducing species), one instance of a deeper connection between ecological and evolutionary dynamics. ## Reading the nullclines: the four outcomes Set $\dot N_1=0$ with $N_1\ne0$: this is the line $N_1+\beta_{12}N_2=K_1$, crossing the $N_1$-axis at $K_1$ and the $N_2$-axis at $K_1/\beta_{12}$. Likewise $\dot N_2=0$ (with $N_2\ne0$) is the line $N_2+\beta_{21}N_1=K_2$, crossing the $N_2$-axis at $K_2$ and the $N_1$-axis at $K_2/\beta_{21}$. The three boundary points $(0,0)$, $(K_1,0)$ and $(0,K_2)$ are always fixed points. A fourth, interior fixed point exists only when the two nullcline segments actually cross inside the positive quadrant; whether they do is what separates the four cases. At the origin both species are rare, and since both $r_i>0$ (each species can survive alone), the origin repels in every direction — a source. Whether $(K_1,0)$ and $(0,K_2)$ attract or repel, and whether an interior fixed point exists at all, comes down to comparing $K_1/\beta_{12}$ against $K_2$, and $K_2/\beta_{21}$ against $K_1$: | $K_1/\beta_{12}$ vs. $K_2$ | $K_2/\beta_{21}$ vs. $K_1$ | Outcome | | --- | --- | --- | | $K_1/\beta_{12}>K_2$ (species 2 barely harms 1) | $K_2/\beta_{21}K_1$ | species 2 wins | | $K_1/\beta_{12}>K_2$ | $K_2/\beta_{21}>K_1$ (both weak) | coexistence | | $K_1/\beta_{12}K_2$, species 2 barely dents species 1's growth; because $K_1>K_2/\beta_{21}$, species 1 crushes species 2's. The two nullclines don't cross inside the positive quadrant, there is no interior fixed point, $(K_1,0)$ is the only stable point, and every trajectory that starts with both species present ends up there. Bistability is the one case where the long-run outcome genuinely depends on where you start, given both species present: the fourth, interior fixed point there is an unstable saddle separating the two basins of attraction. If a species starts at zero abundance, of course, it stays at zero — nothing in the model creates a species from nothing. ## The outcome does not depend on how fast either species grows The classification above only involves the $K_i$ and $\beta_{ij}$; the growth rates $r_1,r_2$ never enter it. They still shape the transient — how a trajectory gets to its fixed point — just not which fixed point it ends at. If species 2 divides much faster than species 1, a trajectory starting with a little of each can swing up close to where species 2 looks dominant, and only later curve back and settle at $(K_1,0)$. Strogatz's book tells this as sheep and rabbits competing for the same grass: the faster-dividing rabbits appear to take over first, but the sheep, more effective at excluding a competitor from the resource, eventually displace them. This is competitive exclusion: when two species compete intensely enough for the same resource, only one survives in the long run, and which one is set by the $K_i,\beta_{ij}$, not by who grew fastest at the start. ## An aside: what changes under noise? A question from the class exposed something the deterministic picture hides. The equations above allow fractional individuals and contain no intrinsic randomness — there is no "one last individual" disappearing. Turn this into a stochastic (Gillespie) simulation the most literal way — put the entire right-hand side in as a single birth propensity — and extinction becomes impossible, because there is no death channel at all. Any honest translation to a birth-death process has to split growth explicitly into a birth rate and a death rate, $r_iN_i \to B_i - D_i$; the deterministic equation is indifferent to how you split it, but the fluctuations are not — more churn (larger $B_i,D_i$ individually, even at the same net rate) means more noise and a higher chance of extinction by chance. Given that split, where is extinction of the losing species most likely in the species-1-wins case? Not near the stable point $(K_1,0)$: the trajectories there always increase in $N_1$ (and so decrease the loser), which means the losing species is at its most vulnerable to being wiped out by chance right at the start, while still rare — not later on, once the outcome has already become clear. ## Many competing species Normalize each species' abundance by its own carrying capacity, $X_i=N_i/K_i$, and collect the competition coefficients into a single matrix $\alpha_{ij}$ with $\alpha_{ii}=1$ (each species alone still follows plain logistic growth, with carrying capacity 1). The competition model generalizes to $$\dot X_i = r_iX_i\left(1-\sum_j \alpha_{ij}X_j\right), \qquad i=1,\dots,N,$$ and, for competitive interactions, $\alpha_{ij}\ge 0$ for all $i\ne j$. Moving fluently between this non-dimensionalized form and the original $N_i,K_i,\beta_{ij}$ version is not just bookkeeping — it is exactly the kind of question ("how does the parameter change if you change the strength of expression") that shows up on exams. For a competitive system like this, several structural facts hold regardless of the specific $\alpha_{ij}$ (stated, not derived, in lecture): - **The unit hypercube traps trajectories.** If every species starts with $0\le X_i(0)\le1$, every species stays inside that range forever. Nothing forbids starting outside the hypercube — "carrying capacity" is not a literal hard ceiling — but starting inside means never leaving. - **The dynamics live on an $(N-1)$-dimensional surface.** Describing every possible trajectory still needs the full $N$ dimensions, since any of the $N$ initial abundances can be anything. But the long-run behaviour — where trajectories actually settle or circulate — occupies one dimension fewer than the full space. - **Continuous trajectories cannot cross themselves.** Combined with the point above, this bounds how many species a genuinely complicated attractor needs: a limit cycle needs two dimensions to draw without self-crossing, so it needs $N\ge3$ competing species; chaos needs three dimensions (a chaotic trajectory has to pass over and under itself, not just around), so it needs $N\ge4$. In a generic dynamical system chaos can already appear with three variables; the extra requirement is specific to this competitive Lotka-Volterra structure. A further result says essentially any dynamics becomes achievable once $N\ge5$. None of this says every four-species competitive system is chaotic — only that it is possible for one to be. What makes it worth pausing on is how little machinery it takes: this is about as simple a model of interacting variables as one can write down, and it is already enough to generate limit cycles and chaos. A brief note on why a *stable* fixed point is harder to rule limit cycles out from than an *unstable* one: a Poincaré–Bendixson-type argument (used earlier for the two-species predator-prey case) runs one direction only. An unstable fixed point, surrounded by a region trajectories cannot leave, guarantees a limit cycle somewhere inside that region. The converse — a stable fixed point rules out a limit cycle — does not follow from that same argument in general; it happens to be true for the specific two-species Lotka-Volterra predator-prey system, provable separately via a divergence-type condition, but it is not a general fact. ## Non-transitive competition: rock-paper-scissors Everything so far has one strategy or species eventually beating another, or the two settling into coexistence or bistability. A non-transitive interaction breaks that pattern: three strategies $X,Y,Z$ where $X$ beats $Y$, $Y$ beats $Z$, and $Z$ beats $X$ — the familiar rock-paper-scissors relation. No strategy is best; each is beaten by exactly one of the other two. This kind of cyclic dominance can, in principle, stabilize diversity that a simple pairwise-dominance argument would otherwise eliminate — especially, the lecture argues, once spatial structure is added. ### Male mating strategies in side-blotched lizards Sinervo and Lively's 1996 *Nature* paper, "The Rock-Paper-Scissors Game and the Evolution of Alternative Male Strategies," studied side-blotched lizards in the mountains outside the Bay Area (Merced County, California). Males come in three genetically encoded, heritable throat colors and mating strategies: orange-throated males ($X$) are aggressive and defend large territories with many females; dark-blue- throated males ($Y$) are less aggressive and defend smaller territories; and yellow-striped "sneaker" males ($Z$) mimic females, hold no territory at all, and instead sneak into other males' territories to mate. Orange beats blue head-to-head — a bigger territory simply means more mates. But orange's territory is too large to defend effectively against sneaking, so the sneakers beat orange. And blue's smaller, easier-to-defend territory catches the sneakers, so blue beats them, closing the cycle. Field data collected over about seven years show the frequencies of the three strategies cycling once around this triangle. ### Colicin warfare in E. coli Kerr et al.'s 2002 *Nature* paper, "Local Dispersal Promotes Biodiversity in a Real-Life Game of Rock-Paper-Scissors," finds the same structure within a single bacterial species. Colicinogenic cells ($X$) carry a plasmid that produces colicin, a toxin that pores other cells' membranes — but the only way colicin is released is by the producing cell bursting open, so this is a costly trait that can never benefit the individual cell that dies. It is supported only by a kin- or group-selection argument, protecting clone-mates that share the plasmid's immunity gene. Sensitive cells ($Y$) pay none of that cost and have no immunity, so colicinogenic cells beat them. Resistant cells ($Z$) carry the immunity gene without the costly lysis step, so they beat the colicinogenic strain. And resistance itself carries a smaller growth cost that sensitive cells don't pay, so sensitive cells beat resistant ones, closing the cycle. Grown together in a well-mixed test tube, the three strains do not coexist: the sensitive strain is wiped out first, essentially outright, once colicin accumulates — a near-total kill rather than the smooth, gradual competitive suppression a Lotka-Volterra interaction term describes. With no sensitive cells left to kill, the colicinogenic strain gains nothing from its costly toxin production and is in turn outcompeted by the resistant strain, which is left alone. But grown on an agar plate divided into roughly twenty patches on a hexagonal grid, seeded with the three strains and propagated for about a week by daily replica-plating (lifting cells with a velvet and pressing them onto a fresh plate), all three strains persisted, each spatially chasing the one it beats — sensitive cells invading resistant territory, resistant invading colicinogenic, colicinogenic invading sensitive — though only the colicinogenic strain's boundary was visible by eye, since the sensitive and resistant strains happened to grow to similar colony density. The lecture is careful about what this does and doesn't show: it is not a general proof that non-transitive interactions cannot coexist in a well-mixed setting — reasonable Lotka-Volterra-style rock-paper-scissors equations exist (in Nowak's book) that spiral into stable coexistence without any spatial structure at all. It shows only that, for these particular three E. coli strains — whose actual dynamics, a strain being essentially killed outright rather than gradually suppressed, are not well captured by a smooth Lotka-Volterra term in the first place — coexistence needs the spatial structure. A follow-up computational study by Erwin Frey, varying how mobile the simulated cells are, found a critical mobility: below it, spatial structure sustains the three-way coexistence; above it, the system behaves like the well-mixed case and diversity is lost. ## Population waves: growth meets diffusion The last topic turns from *what fraction of each species survives* to *how fast a population spreads through space*. Take the logistic growth equation and add diffusion, now written for a population density $n(x,t)$ rather than a total count: $$\frac{\partial n}{\partial t} = rn\left(1-\frac{n}{K}\right) + D\,\frac{\partial^2 n}{\partial x^2}.$$ The diffusion term is a coarse-grained stand-in for however individuals actually move — walking, swimming, being carried — valid over length and time scales much larger than an individual step, and only if the distribution of step sizes is well-behaved enough for a central-limit argument to apply (see the aside on long-tailed dispersal below). Starting from a single founder, or a small seeded patch, the local population grows and saturates at $K$, and a front spreads outward whose shape stays the same over time — a genuine traveling wave, $n(x,t)=f(x-vt)$, moving at a constant velocity $v$. **Getting the velocity by dimensional analysis.** $r$ has units of $1/\text{time}$ and $D$ has units of $\text{length}^2/\text{time}$; $K$ is a density and drops out of the argument entirely (it sets the units of $n$ itself, and rescaling $n$ by $K$ removes it from the equation). The only combination of $r$ and $D$ with units of $\text{length}/\text{time}$ is $\sqrt{rD}$, so $v \propto \sqrt{rD}$. The exact result, first derived by R.A. Fisher in the 1920s — not to describe range expansion, but the spread of a favorable allele through a spatial population, another instance of the same mathematics doing evolutionary and ecological work at once — fixes the constant: $$v = 2\sqrt{rD}.$$ **This is a "pulled" wave.** Faster growth and larger mobility both make the wave move faster, as expected, but — to leading order, in the deterministic regime — the velocity does not depend on $K$, and more surprisingly, it depends on the growth curve $g(n)=\dot n/n$ only through its value at $n=0$, i.e. through $r$ itself. Populations with very different growth-rate curves away from $n=0$, but the same value $g(0)=r$, spread at exactly the same velocity, because it is the sparse leading edge of the wave — where $n$ is small and $g(n)\approx g(0)$ — that sets the pace for the whole front; the front pulls the bulk along behind it. The front decays ahead of the bulk on a characteristic length scale $\sqrt{D/r}$. **Pushed waves.** Front-only reasoning breaks down for a population with a strong Allee effect — a per-capita growth rate that is actually negative at low density, up to some threshold, because individuals do worse when rare (cooperative growth). Taken at face value, the pulled-wave argument would say such a population cannot expand at all, since its front is dying rather than growing. Yet it still can expand: the expansion is now driven by diffusion out of the dense, healthily-growing bulk behind the front, rather than by growth at the front itself. This qualitatively different regime is a pushed wave — the bulk pushes the front, rather than the front pulling the bulk. The distinction has consequences beyond the velocity. One of the readings (in *Physics Today*) points out that pulled and pushed waves lose genetic diversity at different rates: a pulled wave's dynamics are effectively set by the sparse population right at the low-density edge, giving it a small effective population size and fast loss of heterozygosity, while a pushed wave's dynamics are set by the dense bulk, giving it a larger effective population size and slower loss of diversity. **A caveat on the diffusion approximation.** The whole picture assumes individual movements have a well-behaved (finite-variance, "not long-tailed") step-size distribution, so a central-limit argument lets simple diffusion stand in for the actual motion at large scales. Oskar Hallatschek's work on epidemic spread argues this assumption can fail for human travel: most moves stay local, but a long-distance move (a flight to another continent) has small but non-negligible probability, giving a long-tailed, effectively infinite-variance step-size distribution — and in that regime the simple diffusive picture, and the wave behavior built on it, no longer applies. ## Sources All of this chapter comes from one lecture recording; no slide deck was supplied for this session, so the whiteboard nullcline diagram is reconstructed from the verbal description and the class's clicker responses, not copied from a slide. - Two-species competition model, nullclines, the four outcomes, and the mapping to frequency-dependent selection: transcript `3eizij6qncy`, [00:00]-[19:50]. - Independence from growth rates and the sheep/rabbits competitive-exclusion story: [17:48]-[19:50], referring to a chapter in Strogatz's *Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos* (not supplied). - The stochastic-extinction discussion: [20:03]-[24:44]. - The normalized $N$-species model and the dimension results for limit cycles, chaos, and the Poincaré-Bendixson aside: [24:44]-[37:08]. - Non-transitive interactions, general framing: [37:08]-[38:28]. - Side-blotched lizard mating strategies: [38:28]-[47:35], from Sinervo and Lively, "The Rock-Paper- Scissors Game and the Evolution of Alternative Male Strategies," *Nature*, 1996 (not supplied, described in lecture only). - Colicin rock-paper-scissors in E. coli: [47:35]-[1:01:28], from Kerr et al., "Local Dispersal Promotes Biodiversity in a Real-Life Game of Rock-Paper-Scissors," *Nature*, 2002 (not supplied; the class had read it directly). Erwin Frey's computational follow-up on mobility and coexistence is referenced but not supplied. - Population waves, dimensional analysis, and the Fisher velocity: [1:01:28]-[1:14:39]. - Pulled vs. pushed waves and effective population size: [1:14:39]-[1:20:37], referencing a *Physics Today* article on loss of heterozygosity in range expansions (not supplied) and Oskar Hallatschek's work on long-tailed dispersal kernels in epidemic spread (not supplied). - Also referenced but not supplied: Martin Nowak's book (the frequency-dependent-selection mapping, and a Lotka-Volterra rock-paper-scissors example with stable coexistence), and R.A. Fisher's original 1920s derivation of the wave equation.
